To maim someone means to injure them so severely that a part of their body is permanently destroyed, lost, or disabled — but they survive. The person lives on, but they are left fundamentally and irreversibly altered.

This is the heart of the word, and it sets it apart from ordinary injury words: the damage does not heal. A broken arm heals. A deep cut heals. But when someone is maimed, that chapter of their body's wholeness is closed forever.

Maiming always involves one or more of these outcomes:

Loss of a body part — A limb (arm, leg, hand, foot) or organ (eye, ear) is destroyed or amputated as a result of the injury. A soldier who loses his leg to a landmine has been maimed.

Loss of function — The body part is still physically there, but it no longer works. A hand that is crushed so severely it can never grip or move again — that is maiming, even if the hand is still attached.

Permanent, severe disfigurement — The person's body or face is so badly damaged that it is irrevocably altered. This falls under maiming because the destruction is permanent.
The Three Things That Make "Maim" Unique

Understanding what separates "maim" from similar words is crucial.

1. The person survives.
This is non-negotiable. You cannot maim a dead person. Maiming is precisely about a person who lives on with the damage. If someone dies from their injuries, we would say they were killed, not maimed. Maiming is, in a grim way, about the aftermath — the long life lived with permanent loss.

2. The damage is permanent.
This is the sharpest edge of the word. General injury words like hurt, wound, or injure don't carry this weight — they can describe things that fully recover. Maiming cannot be reversed, treated away, or grown back. It is forever.

3. It affects the body's capability or wholeness.
Maiming isn't just about pain or even severe injury in a general sense — it specifically removes something from the person: a limb, a sense, a function, or their former physical form. The person after the maiming is less physically able or whole than the person before it.

"Maim" works in both situations.

Someone can be maimed deliberately — a violent attacker who destroys a victim's hand to prevent them from ever working again has intentionally maimed them. Historically and in legal contexts, maiming often carries this meaning of deliberate, cruel harm.

Someone can also be maimed accidentally — a factory worker whose arm is caught in heavy machinery, or a person badly injured in a car crash. The word applies regardless of intent; what matters is the permanent, disabling result.

That said, "maim" carries a weight and gravity that makes it feel more at home in serious, often violent contexts — war, crime, catastrophic accidents. You wouldn't casually use it for a minor mishap.
Sentence Examples That Show the Word in Action

• The explosion maimed dozens of civilians, leaving many without limbs.
  • He was maimed in the factory accident — his right hand never recovered.
  • The boxer's career was over; a brutal punch had maimed his vision permanently.
  • Landmines continue to kill and maim people long after wars have ended.
  • She was maimed for life after the acid attack.

Notice how in each case, the victim is alive — but permanently and seriously changed.

You will frequently encounter the phrase "kill or maim." This pairing exists precisely because it covers the two worst possible outcomes of violence or danger: death, and permanent disabling injury. When something is said to be able to "kill or maim," it means it can either end your life or leave you permanently and gravely damaged. This phrase is common in legal writing, military contexts, and safety warnings.
One Final Way to Lock It In

Think of it this way: if an injury is survivable but permanently steals something from your body, that is maiming. The body carries the evidence of what happened — not as a scar that fades, but as an absence or a dysfunction that stays for life.
